content: 1. A study published in Value Health in 2011 (Volume 14, Issue 3, Page A160) compared oncology treatments, but the data was deemed insufficient for conclusive analysis. 2. O'Leary, Usher, and Lynch explored the perspectives of key stakeholders on generic substitution in Ireland. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2013 (Volume 16, Issue 7, Page A460), highlighted insufficient data to draw definitive conclusions. 3. Orlewski et al. examined the impact of Polish human insulin (Gensulin) on public payer expenditures between 2001 and 2013. Their study, published in Value Health in 2013 (Volume 16, Issue 7, Page A451), also reported insufficient data. 4. Park et al. analyzed the differential effects of two pharmaceutical cost-containment policies on outpatient prescription drug expenditures in Korea. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2014 (Volume 17, Issue 3, Page A14), indicated insufficient data for robust conclusions. 5. Park SE and colleagues investigated factors influencing the reimbursement price of new drugs after the introduction of a positive list system. Their study, published in Value Health in 2012 (Volume 15, Issue 4, Page A24), reported insufficient data. 6. Park Y et al. conducted a literature review on factors affecting price and competition in the global pharmaceutical market. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2016 (Volume 19, Issue 3, Page A265), highlighted insufficient data. 7. Patikorn et al. proposed strategies to improve access to high-cost anticancer drugs, with lessons for ASEAN countries. Their study, published in Value Health in 2018 (Volume 21, Pages S20-S21), reported insufficient data. 8. Petrov and Hubenov discussed the introduction of formal risk-sharing agreements (RSAs) as a potential solution for sustainable pharmaceutical expenditures in Bulgaria. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2015 (Volume 18, Issue 7, Pages A571-2), indicated insufficient data. 9. Puig-Peiró et al. reviewed patient access schemes, flexible pricing, and risk-sharing agreements for medicines. Their study, published in Value Health in 2011 (Volume 14, Issue 7, Page A243), reported insufficient data. 10. Putignano et al. assessed the impact of cost-containment policies on the biosimilars market. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2014 (Volume 17, Issue 7, Page A415), indicated insufficient data. 11. Qiu et al. examined the inequity of orphan drug prices in Europe. Their study, published in Value Health in 2018 (Volume 21, Pages S461-S62), reported insufficient data. 12. Raftery analyzed the multiple sclerosis risk-sharing scheme, describing it as a costly failure. This analysis was published in BMJ in 2010 (Volume 340, Pages 1-6). 13. Raftery JP explored cost-effectiveness in healthcare, comparing individual drug evaluations by NICE with budget cuts under PPRS. His findings, published in Value Health in 2014 (Volume 17, Issue 7, Page A410), reported insufficient data. 14. Relakis et al. conducted a systematic review on the impacts of strict pharmaceutical price controls. Their study, published in Value Health in 2013 (Volume 16, Issue 7, Page A486), indicated insufficient data. 15. Rémuzat et al. identified key drivers for the market penetration of biosimilars in Europe. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2016 (Volume 19, Issue 7, Page A497), reported insufficient data. 16. Rong and Sun studied the impact of pricing policy on short-supplied drugs in Shandong, China, using an interrupted time series approach. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2018 (Volume 21, Page S44), indicated insufficient data. 17. Samjoo et al. provided insights into the Pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance's decision not to collectively negotiate drug pricing. Their study, published in Value Health in 2016 (Volume 19, Issue 3, Page A171), reported insufficient data. 18. Sandhu and Heidenreich discussed the benefits and challenges of performance-linked reimbursement plans for novel drugs, using sacubitril-valsartan as a case study. Their findings were published in Circ Cardiovasc Qual in 2018. 19. Saylan et al. evaluated the impact of health policy changes on the unit sales of the top five ATC1 pharmaceutical groups in Turkey. Their study, published in Value Health in 2014 (Volume 17, Issue 7, Page A411), reported insufficient data. 20. Schmidt and Mueller provided insights from early benefit assessments under AMNOG in Germany. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2012 (Volume 15, Issue 7, Page A311), indicated insufficient data. 21. Schneider et al. discussed the methodological challenges of early benefit assessments for orphan drugs in Germany and their implications for reimbursement pricing. Their study, published in Value Health in 2016 (Volume 19, Issue 3, Page A281), reported insufficient data. 22. His findings were published in Clin Ther in 2013 (Volume 35, Issue 8, Page e129). 23. Seitlinger and Flostrand analyzed post-LOE pricing dynamics in oncology, focusing on mandatory price discounts and generic uptake. Their study, published in Value Health in 2018 (Volume 21, Page S55), reported insufficient data. 24. Sherwin et al. analyzed pricing and market access for orphan drugs in China, considering national and provincial policies. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2016 (Volume 19, Issue 7, Page A835), indicated insufficient data. 25. Spillane et al. reviewed the recently introduced generic substitution and reference pricing system in Ireland, assessing its impact on generic dispensing, savings, and co-payment burdens. Their findings were published in Pharmacoepidemiol Drug Saf in 2016 (Volume 25, Pages 356-57). 26. Szmurlo et al. reviewed the pricing of medicines in Poland, analyzing the effects of a new law on reimbursement costs over two years. Their study, published in Value Health in 2014 (Volume 17, Issue 7, Pages A413-4), reported insufficient data. 27. Teale et al. explored the sustainability of the European biosimilar medicines market, considering competition, interchangeability, procurement, and pricing. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2018 (Volume 21, Page S154), indicated insufficient data. 28. Teixeira et al. analyzed pharmaceutical expenditure policies and their impact in Portugal. Their study, published in Value Health in 2011 (Volume 14, Issue 7, Page A345), reported insufficient data. 29. Timm et al. assessed the influence of patient access schemes on NICE appraisal decisions in the UK. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2011 (Volume 14, Issue 3, Page A19), indicated insufficient data. 30. Tsakalogiannis et al. examined stakeholder views on the role of HTA and RSAs in pharmaceutical policy in Greece. Their study, published in Value Health in 2016 (Volume 19, Issue 7, Page A466), reported insufficient data. 31. Tuffaha and Scuffham evaluated patient access to novel cancer drugs in Australia, questioning whether progress had been made. Their findings were published in Asia Pac J Clin Oncol in 2017 (Volume 13, Pages 84-85). 32. Tuna and Kockaya analyzed the impact of biosimilar penetration on the prices of reference biotechnology products in Turkey. Their study, published in Value Health in 2015 (Volume 18, Issue 7, Page A535), reported insufficient data. 33. Vasileva et al. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2015 (Volume 18, Issue 7, Page A534), indicated insufficient data. 34. Victor Rodrigues Wehner et al. analyzed the outcomes of a Brazilian pharmaceutical regulation resolution. Their study, published in Value Health in 2012 (Volume 15, Issue 4, Page A15), reported insufficient data. 35. Wettermark et al. assessed the impact of European reforms encouraging the prescribing of generic statins. Their findings were published in Pharmacoepidemiol Drug Saf in 2009 (Volume 18, Supplement 1, Page S147). 36. Yu et al. conducted a systematic review of performance-based risk-sharing arrangements in the United States. Their findings were published in J Manag Care Spec Pharm in 2017 (Volume 23, Pages S93). 37. Zhang et al. analyzed biosimilar market policies in China. Their study, published in Value Health in 2014 (Volume 17, Issue 7, Page A800), reported insufficient data. 38. Zhou et al. reviewed the effects of reference pricing on pharmaceuticals. Their findings, published in Value Health in 2014 (Volume 17, Issue 7, Page A787), indicated insufficient data. 39. Ziai Buetas et al. examined payer strategies for purchasing complex biosimilars under a new biologic paradigm. Their study, published in Value Health in 2014 (Volume 17, Issue 7, Page A388), reported insufficient data. 40. Abbas et al. reviewed orphan drug policies across different countries. Their findings were published in J Pharm Health Serv Res in 2019 (Volume 10, Issue 3, Pages 295-302). 41. Abdel Rida et al. conducted a systematic review of pharmaceutical pricing policies in developing countries. Their findings were published in J Pharm Health Serv Res in 2017 (Volume 8, Issue 4, Pages 213-26). 42. Acosta et al. reviewed the effects of reference pricing and other pharmaceutical pricing policies. Their findings were published in the Cochrane Database Syst Rev in 2014 (Issue 10, Article CD005979). 43. Babar et al. compared patient access to medicines in two countries with similar health systems but differing pharmaceutical policies. Their findings were published in Res Social Adm Pharm in 2019 (Volume 15, Issue 3, Pages 231-43). 44. Ball reviewed pharmaceutical pricing policies and interventions, focusing on the regulation of mark-ups in the supply chain. This working paper was published in Amsterdam in 2011. 45. Barros analyzed pharmaceutical policies in European countries, with findings published in Adv Health Econ Health Serv Res in 2010 (Volume 22, Pages 3-27). 46. Deng et al. assessed the zero-markup drug reform in China, considering policy diffusion perspectives. Their findings were published in Int J Health Plann Manage in 2018 (Volume 33, Issue 4, Pages e918-e29). 47. Hay discussed competitive tendering for purchasing factor concentrates in the 21st century. His findings were published in Haemophilia in 2013 (Volume 19, Issue 5, Pages 660-67). 48. Hinrichs et al. conducted a rapid evidence assessment on NHS procurement and supply chain management. Their findings were published in Health Services and Delivery Research in 2014. 49. Kötting and May compared centralized price regulation with individual contract discount agreements in Germany. Their findings were published in Gesundheitswesen in 2008 (Volume 13, Issue 4, Pages 191-94). 50. Lee et al. conducted a systematic review of reference pricing and its implications for US prescription drug spending. Their findings were published in Am J Manag Care in 2012 (Volume 18, Issue 11, Pages e429-37). 51. Morgan et al. compared tiered formularies and reference pricing policies in a systematic review. Their findings were published in Open Med in 2009 (Volume 3, Issue 3, Pages e131-9). 52. Parkinson et al. reviewed disinvestment and value-based purchasing strategies for pharmaceuticals internationally. Their findings were published in Pharmacoeconomics in 2015 (Volume 33, Issue 9, Pages 905-24). 53. Puig-Junoy reviewed the impact of European pharmaceutical price regulation on generic price competition. His findings were published in Pharmacoeconomics in 2010 (Volume 28, Issue 8, Pages 649-63). 54. Sanderson et al. synthesized theoretical and empirical literature to enhance NHS procurement and supply chain management practices. Their findings were published in Health Services and Delivery Research in 2015. 55. Silvestri et al. reviewed the impact of price display on provider ordering behavior. Their findings were published in J Hosp Med in 2016 (Volume 11, Issue 1, Pages 65-76). 56. Stadhouders et al. reviewed effective healthcare cost-containment policies. Their findings were published in Health Policy in 2019 (Volume 123, Issue 1, Pages 71-79). 57. Swartenbroekx et al. analyzed incentives for biosimilar market penetration in Belgium and five European countries. Their findings were published in J Pharm Belg in 2014 (Issue 4, Pages 36-46). 58. Wettstein and Boes reviewed the effectiveness of national pricing policies for patent-protected pharmaceuticals in OECD countries. Their findings were published in Appl Health Econ Health Policy in 2019 (Volume 17, Issue 2, Pages 143-62). 59. Yu et al. conducted a systematic review of performance-based risk-sharing arrangements for pharmaceutical products in the United States. Their findings were published in J Manag Care Spec Pharm in 2017 (Volume 23, Issue 10, Pages 1028-40). 60. Bussières et al. compared activity-based pricing and financing of expensive drugs in France. Their findings were published in Can J Hosp Pharm in 2016 (Volume 69, Issue 2, Pages 138-43). This list represents a comprehensive overview of studies and reviews addressing various aspects of pharmaceutical pricing, market dynamics, and healthcare policies across different countries and regions. Many of these studies reported insufficient data or methodological challenges, highlighting the complexity of evaluating pharmaceutical policies and their outcomes.
